record.title: Trajectory-aware selection reports lower-error SWE-agent regression estimates at one-tenth benchmark size
record.summary: A September 21, 2026 paper proposes selecting a small regression-test subset for software-engineering agents from prior task outcomes and sanitized trajectory embeddings. Across 76 configurations and three code-agent regression scenarios using SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Rebench, the authors report that their 10% deterministic subset kept median resolve-rate estimation error below 5% and reduced token consumption from 3.44 billion to about 345 million in the analyzed multi-model runs. They analyze 31,779 trajectories from 58 runs across five agent frameworks and use temporal splits so selection uses earlier runs than evaluation runs. The method requires prior full-run history, dataset-specific trajectory sanitization and refresh when behavior changes; evidence is limited to code-repair benchmarks and the paper has no independent reproduction in this record.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that selecting 10% of SWE-bench tasks using historical outcome groups and geometric selection over sanitized trajectory embeddings kept median resolve-rate estimation error below 5%, with 90% lower token use than the full benchmark in their evaluated runs. The study covers SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Rebench across same-setup reruns, model/configuration changes and framework changes. This is a paper-reported estimate on those datasets, not evidence that a 10% subset can replace full evaluation across other domains or after large architecture shifts.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper links a replication package, but no independent execution or reproduction has been performed in this record.
Evaluation covers SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Rebench code repair; transfer to web navigation, general tool-use, scientific or other agent benchmarks is not established.

The subset depends on historical trajectories and may miss unusual failures after large agent architecture or behavior changes; the paper recommends refreshing embeddings when typical behavior changes.

brief.importance_rationale: If replicated in active SWE-agent development, a representative 10% task subset that preserves resolve-rate estimates while cutting most evaluation token use could make regression checks frequent enough to improve iteration speed and evaluation coverage. A 5 reflects meaningful engineering/evaluation impact limited to code-repair benchmarks, paper-reported evidence and dependence on prior full-run trajectories.
limitations: The result is restricted to software repair benchmarks, SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Rebench; external validity beyond coding agents is untested.
Subset selection requires at least one prior full run and uses prior trajectories and outcome groups; embeddings and strata may become stale after behavior or benchmark changes.
The paper evaluates error in estimating full-suite resolve rate, not preservation of every rare failure mode or all safety-relevant properties.
Results are authors’ offline analyses; no independent reproduction has been conducted in this record.

For the 1,000 synthetic distributions sampled from 500 instances, distributions overlap. The authors note that this makes Wilcoxon p-values optimistic; they also report effect sizes and checks across difficulty levels.

The 10% / 90% headline is an evaluated token-cost regime, not a universal guarantee: the selected centroid subset used 10.48% of token cost on average, while random 10% subsets ranged 5.7–15.0% across the widest spread.
brief.summary: A September 21, 2026 paper proposes selecting a small regression-test subset for software-engineering agents from prior task outcomes and sanitized trajectory embeddings. Across 76 configurations and three code-agent regression scenarios using SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Rebench, the authors report that their 10% deterministic subset kept median resolve-rate estimation error below 5% and reduced token consumption from 3.44 billion to about 345 million in the analyzed multi-model runs. They analyze 31,779 trajectories from 58 runs across five agent frameworks and use temporal splits so selection uses earlier runs than evaluation runs. The method requires prior full-run history, dataset-specific trajectory sanitization and refresh when behavior changes; evidence is limited to code-repair benchmarks and the paper has no independent reproduction in this record.

technical.claimed_result: Across the authors’ SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Rebench evaluations, 10% trajectory-aware subsets reportedly kept median resolve-rate estimation error below 5%. In the six-run multi-model cost analysis, a selected 10% subset used about 345M tokens versus 3.44B for all 500 instances (about 90% reduction). The paper reports improvements against typical and high-error baseline draws across three regression scenarios.
technical.demonstrated_result: No independent demonstration is recorded. These findings are CLAIMED by the paper authors from offline benchmark analyses of public agent trajectories.
technical.implementation_status: An offline benchmark-selection pipeline is described and a replication package is linked; adoption in a production CI system is not evaluated.
technical.mechanism: The method groups tasks by outcomes from prior full runs, sanitizes trajectory records to remove explicit result leakage, embeds behavior traces and deterministically chooses geometrically representative instances within outcome groups. It evaluates resolve rate on that subset as an estimate of the full suite, with temporal splits across earlier and later runs.
technical.regime: Software-agent code-repair evaluation on SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Rebench. Three scenarios cover same-configuration reruns, model/configuration changes and framework changes. Study uses 31,779 trajectories from 58 runs across five agent frameworks; subset selection uses historical full-run outcome/trajectory data and later runs for temporal evaluation.
technical.reproducibility: The authors link a dataset, parser, sanitization and selection implementation. This review did not execute the package or independently reproduce the reported estimates.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares with outcome-stratified random selection and other random, embedding, clustering and hybrid methods. It reports the centroid-based trajectory embedding method as best among the evaluated configurations; at 5%/10%, error gains are measured relative to typical and 95th-percentile baseline draws.

brief.title: Trajectory-aware selection reports lower-error SWE-agent regression estimates at one-tenth benchmark size
brief.why_it_matters: Full SWE-agent benchmark runs are expensive because each issue triggers many model calls and tool steps. A subset that estimates resolve rate with lower error at a fraction of task count could support more frequent regression checks between full runs. The practical claim is bounded to the paper’s two code-repair benchmarks and historical-trajectory setup; it does not establish that organizations can safely abandon full evaluations.
